fetched_contents.text: Microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis of hydroxyapatite from fermented fish by-product for removal of lead from contaminated water | Beni-Suef University Journal of Basic and Applied Sciences 1 Introduction Lead (Pb) contamination in potable and industrial wastewater poses a persistent global health and environmental challenge. High Pb concentrations have been linked to neurological damage, impaired cognitive development, and long-term ecological harm [1]. Traditional remediation methods such as chemical precipitation, ion exchange resins, and activated carbon adsorption have shown varying degrees of success, but their widespread deployment is often constrained by high operational costs, secondary waste production, and limited reusability capacities [2]. Consequently, there is a growing demand for innovative, economically viable, and environmentally benign materials that can efficiently capture lead ions under realistic conditions, especially those derived from by-products and waste streams, to reduce production costs and environmental impacts [3]. Among the diverse adsorbent materials used for water purification, hydroxyapatite (HAp; Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) has gained significant attention as an environmentally friendly solution for removing pollutants from water [4]. HAp is composed primarily of calcium and phosphate, which can be sourced from both synthetic methods and biogenic wastes like chicken bones, eggshells, and fish bones. HAp has demonstrated remarkable efficiency in binding with various heavy metals such as lead (Pb2+), cadmium (Cd2+), copper (Cu2+), and arsenic (As5+) through mechanisms like ion exchange and dissolution–precipitation [5]. Synthetic HAp can be produced via chemical routes; however, such approaches frequently rely on energy-intensive conditions or harsh chemicals, potentially undermining their sustainability advantages [6]. Consequently, the search for alternative, cost-effective, and environmentally benign raw materials for HAp production remains a critical area of research [7]. This has urged a growing interest in converting biogenic waste into valuable HAp, a strategy that aligns with circular-economy principles by turning potential pollutants into functional materials [8]. Thailand is one of Southeast Asia’s leading producers of fermented fish products such as Pla-ra. The processing activities generate substantial amounts of by-products, most notably fish bones, which are often discarded as waste. Accumulation of this waste poses persistent environmental and disposal challenges. Because the fermented fish bone waste retains residual flesh, proteins, and lipids, their decomposition releases a high-strength leachate rich in soluble organics (high BOD/COD), nutrients, and fats. Uncontrolled discharge can rapidly depress dissolved oxygen and degrade water quality. Under anaerobic conditions, putrefaction also releases strong odor and nuisance gases like ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, and volatile mercaptans, often prompting community complaints and regulatory action. Additionally, the waste’s high salinity inhibits conventional biological treatment by suppressing microbial activity and reducing removal efficiency. From a resource recovery perspective, however, these same fish bones are intrinsically rich in calcium and phosphorus, making them an excellent precursor for HAp. Converting the waste into HAp transform liability into a value-added material, providing a low-cost adsorbent for water treatment while mitigating odor, and leachate generation and reducing landfill pressures, this valorization pathway aligns with circular-economy principles and green chemistry approaches by closing material loops, reducing on mined precursors, and lowering the environmental footprint of both waste management and water purification. Technologically, hydrothermal processes can effectively convert calcium-rich biogenic materials such as eggshells, animal bones, and fish bones into high-quality HAp with tunable crystallinity, porosity, and particle morphology [9]. Building on this foundation, microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis delivers volumetric, homogeneous heating that accelerates nucleation and crystal growth, enabling shorter reaction times and lower energy input than conventional hydrothermal heating [10]. With microwave-assisted hydrothermal processing, it may be possible to produce high-quality HAp from fish bone waste under milder conditions [11], potentially enhancing the adsorption kinetics, capacity, and reusability of the final material. Despite these environmental liabilities and the clear promise of resource recovery, a focused knowledge gap remains for fermented fish bone waste specifically. Most studies on biogenic HAp have used non-fermented bones or other calcium-rich precursors [12], leaving the unique chemistry of fermented residues largely unexamined. This underexplored feedstock therefore presents a compelling direction for advancing sustainable materials. Moreover, while the adsorption capabilities of biogenic HAp have been well-documented [13], comparatively few investigations have systematically examined how synthesis conditions, especially microwave-assisted hydrothermal parameters and the resulting Ca/P ratios in HAp affect the physicochemical properties of the HAp and its Pb removal performance. fetched_contents.text: Hydrothermal synthesis of hydroxyapatite powders using Response Surface Methodology (RSM) Abstract Hydroxyapatite (HAp)—[Ca10 (PO4)6(OH) 2] has a similar chemical composition to bone material, making it the main mineral supplement in bone-making. Due to its high biocompatibility, hydroxyapatite is widely used in the repair of bone deficiencies and in the production of dental or orthopedic implants. In this research, hydroxyapatite nanopowder was synthesized using a hydrothermal technique. Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were used to investigate the chemical structure and morphology of the synthesized hydroxyapatite powder. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was used to evaluate the phase analysis of HAp nanopowder. In addition, bioactivity HAp assessment was conducted by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) attached with Energy Dispersive X-Ray Spectroscopy (EDX) analysis. Response Surface Methodology (RSM) with central composite design (CCD) was used in order to determine the optimal conditions for yield, size, and crystallinity. Three independent variables (pH, temperature, and hydrothermal treatment time) were investigated. The yield was observed to increase in alkaline conditions; pH showed the greatest influence on the yield, size, and crystallinity of the synthesized hydroxyapatite, based on Analysis of Variance. The results of bioactivity evaluation are showed high bioactivity due to the formation of apatite on the surface of the synthesized nanopowder. Introduction Calcium phosphate is one of the main mineral components of the skeleton, making it an ideal material for bone grafts in bone tissue engineering [1]. Due to the high biocompatibility and biological activity of calcium phosphate, applications to nanomaterial structures are currently widely investigated [2, 3]. Recently, hydroxyapatite (HAp) has been used in the medical sciences as an important and widely applicable bioceramic, similar to the mineral phase of human hard tissue. This similarity between the chemical composite of hydroxyapatite and bone is the main factor in its bioactivity, its ability to stimulate bone growth, and its therapeutic effects [4, 5]. Hydroxyapatite has been widely synthesized at a nanoscale. Various methods have been used to produce hydroxyapatite nanocrystals, which, depending on the method, generate various products with different structures, apparent features, and crystalline rates. The main HAp synthesis techniques are wet chemical methods and dry reactions [6–11]. Dry reaction methods include solid-state reactions and mechanochemical methods, whereas wet reaction methods include chemical sedimentation, hydrolysis reactions, sol-gel, hydrothermal, emulation, and sonochemical methods. Wet methods allow the size and morphology of nanoparticles to be controlled and are therefore promising techniques for nanoparticle production [12]. The main advantage of ceramic materials synthesized using hydrothermal methods compared to others, such as sol-gel synthesis, is that relatively low temperatures are required to produce the ceramic body [13]. The hydrothermal process is a wet chemical technique able to direct the formation of complex oxide powders with high crystallinity, making it the most popular method used to prepare hydroxyapatite nanoparticles. The advantage of this method, especially in the synthesis of hydroxyapatite powders, is that no hydroxyl defects are produced in the structure. Hydrothermal processes usually work with a chemical reaction in an aqueous solution at high temperature and pressure. Due to its high biocompatibility, this has become a favored technique for material production [14]. Several parameters determine the synthesis of hydroxyapatite nanoparticles. Multiple tests and considerable time are required to determine the optimal conditions of synthesis [15]. Parameters such as temperature, the time of hydrothermal reaction, and the pH of the solution play a significant role in the synthesis of hydroxyapatite nanoparticles with desired properties. Experimental statistical methods such as Response Surface Methodology (RSM) can be used to investigate the effect of these parameters (i.e. pH, hydrothermal reaction time, and temperature). Response surface methods are a set of statistical and mathematical methods that may be used for optimization and modelling and can also evaluate the interactions of multiple variables [15]. In this research, the RSM method with Central Composite Design (CCD) was used to find out the most influential process parameters on the reaction yield, nanoparticle size, and degree of crystallinity of prepared hydroxyapatite nanoparticles. The parameters studied were pH, reaction temperature, and the time of hydrothermal treatment. Materials and methods Materials The raw materials used in this work included calcium nitrate tetrahydrate (Ca (NO3)2.4H2O) and diammonium hydrogen phosphate ((NH4)2HPO4). Ammonia solution (NH3) and nitric acid (HNO3) for adjusting pH were also used. All chemicals were obtained from Merck. Experimental design The effects of pH, hydrothermal temperature, and time on the obtained hydroxyapatite were investigated via Response Surface Methodology (RSM) with Central Composite Design (CCD). This material has been an object of research aiming its use in biomaterials as bone replacement option for biomedical applications. In this investigation, the synthesis of hydroxyapatite was studied by the Hydrothermal (HT) and Microwave Irradiation (MW) methods. Here, parameters such as pH (9 and 11) and synthesis time were varied, and residue of chicken eggshell was used as calcium precursor. The obtained powders were characterized by X-ray Diffraction (XRD), Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), Dispersive Energy X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS), and Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM). The results showed that the material synthesized when the pH reached the value of 9 which generated less carbonated powders than those with pH of 11. The Hydrothermal method presented more satisfactory morphological results according to the TEM analysis. This procedure was considered more suitable as a route to obtain hydroxyapatite as biomaterial. Resumen La hidroxiapatita es el principal componente mineral inorgánico de huesos y dientes. Este material ha sido objeto de investigación dirigida a su uso en biomateriales como sustituto óseo en aplicaciones biomédicas. En este trabajo, se estudió la síntesis de hidroxiapatita utilizando los métodos hidrotermal (HT) y de irradiación de microondas (MW), variando parámetros como el pH (9 y 11) y el tiempo de síntesis, utilizando como precursor de calcio, el residuo de la cáscara de huevo de gallina. Los sólidos (polvo) obtenidos se caracterizaron por difracción de rayos X (DRX), espectroscopía infrarroja por transformada de Fourier (FTIR), espectroscopía de energía dispersiva (EDS) y microscopía electrónica de transmisión (MET). Los resultados mostraron que el material sintetizado a pH 9 generó polvos menos carbonatados que aquellos obtenidos a pH 11. El método hidrotérmico presentó resultados morfológicos más satisfactorios según el análisis de MET. fetched_contents.text: Comparative study of microwave-assisted and hydrothermal hydroxyapatite synthesis from neutralization slag: Optimization, energy, and adsorption Introduction In the vanadium industry, vanadium-containing leachate is generally obtained through acid leaching, with a pH value below 0.5 [1]. The vanadium concentration in this leachate is low, ranging from 1 to 2 g/L [2], necessitating extraction and reverse extraction processes to enrich the vanadium element and obtain a higher-purity vanadium product [3,4]. To achieve extraction conditions that meet the required pH range of 1.8–2.0 for the P204 extractant, neutralization with lime slurry (Ca(OH)2/CaO) is typically necessary [[5], [6], [7], [8]]. During this process, a neutralization slag (NS) is formed, primarily composed of calcium sulfate, along with trace impurities such as iron, aluminum, and magnesium. It is estimated that 90–130 kg of NS can be generated per 1000 L of leachate neutralization, indicating a high yield [9]. Currently, the industrial disposal of NS primarily involves storage [10], which consumes a considerable amount of land and poses a potential environmental risk due to the lack of effective recycling and treatment of solid waste [11]. Additionally, large amounts of high-fluoride wastewater are produced during vanadium smelting, posing a potential risk of fluoride pollution [12]. Fluoride pollution mainly affects soil and water resources [13], accumulating over time and posing a threat to human health and the environment [14]. Hydroxyapatite (HAP), an inorganic material renowned for its remarkable ion-exchange capability [15,16], has been established as an effective adsorbent for fluoride removal from contaminated water sources [17,18]. This is attributed to its capacity to engage in ion exchange reactions with fluoride ions in solution, along with its impressive adsorption capacity and efficiency [[19], [20], [21]]. Furthermore, HAP boasts a porous structure, enabling it to adsorb a diverse array of heavy metal ions present in wastewater, including cadmium (Cd) [22], chromium (Cr) [23], arsenic (As) [22], lead uranium (Ur) [24], and others, thereby mitigating or eliminating their environmental risks. Previous studies have demonstrated the feasibility of synthesizing homogeneous HAP from NS using hydrothermal methods, without the need for surfactants [1,9]. However, several limitations of this hydrothermal synthesis process have been identified. Firstly, particle agglomeration can occur, hindering reactions and reducing the specific surface area of the product, which negatively impacts its performance [25]. Secondly, the reaction time is considerably long, exceeding 90 min excluding heating and cooling, and requiring temperatures exceeding 120 °C. Furthermore, the hydrothermal reaction vessel has a limited capacity per run, resulting in unsatisfactory saturation adsorption performance of the product, thereby increasing the synthesis cost [26]. Apart from hydrothermal methods, alternative manufacturing techniques for HAP have been reported, which encompass deposition [27,28], sol-gel [29,30], and microemulsion procedures [31,32]. These techniques are offered as additional options for the production of HAP. Although traditional synthetic reaction approaches possess their advantages, they are also exhibited to have limitations, such as slow reaction rates and high energy consumption. To enhance reaction efficiency, physical interventions can be employed [33], with microwaves and ultrasounds being commonly used techniques [34,35]. Among these, microwave intervention can facilitate chemical reactions due to its ability to pass through the surface of an object and transfer heat to its interior, thereby reducing the time and temperature required for the reaction process [36,37]. Furthermore, the thermal effect of microwaves is augmented to enhance intermolecular forces [38], leading to faster and more efficient reactions, making it a promising technology for HAP synthesis [39,40]. The potential drawbacks of the microwave method, include uneven temperature distribution, precise parameter control challenges, equipment damage risks, and elevated production costs. Nevertheless, it also presents advantages, such as superior product purity, shortened synthesis time, the use of ordinary glass containers, and lower energy consumption when compared to the hydrothermal method. In this study, a new microwave-assisted process is proposed for the efficient synthesis of hydroxyapatite (HAP) from vanadium industrial neutralization slag (NS), with the main objective of obtaining HAP with high purity and excellent adsorption properties. The synthesis conditions are optimized by modulating the microwave power, time, temperature, and raw material particle size to produce HAP with desirable properties. Response surface optimization technique is used to analyze and optimize various reaction parameters to promote an energy efficient production process. The results of this study will provide valuable insights into the efficient synthesis of high-performance HAP and potential applications. Microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis improves the synthesis of hydroxyapatite mainly by altering the heating mechanism, accelerating nucleation and crystal growth, and optimizing synthesis parameters that are otherwise difficult to control in conventional hydrothermal synthesis.

The most direct process difference is heating mode: conventional hydrothermal synthesis uses bulk heating through the vessel wall, which can produce uneven temperature distribution and long reaction times, whereas microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis delivers volumetric, homogeneous heating that accelerates reaction kinetics [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that microwave-assisted hydrothermal processing enables shorter reaction times and lower energy input than conventional hydrothermal heating [N1-F1]. In the comparative hydrothermal and microwave irradiation study, the hydrothermal method is described as requiring prolonged periods of time, while microwave irradiation can reach the required treatment temperature in fewer minutes [N3-F3]. Another comparative study reports that the microwave hydrothermal method has fast heating speed, sensitive temperature control, and the ability to shorten synthesis time compared to the traditional hydrothermal method [N3-R2]. This means microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis is not merely a variation of hydrothermal synthesis; it changes the energy transfer mechanism from external heating to internal volumetric heating, which can fundamentally alter the reaction dynamics.

Microwave heating affects nucleation and crystal growth by promoting faster and more uniform heat transfer. The evidence states that microwave-assisted hydrothermal processing accelerates nucleation and crystal growth, enabling shorter reaction times and lower energy input [N1-F1]. In the eggshell-based hydroxyapatite synthesis, the study notes that the microwave irradiation method generally produces smaller particle size, good purity, and closer size distribution [N3-F3]. The same study also reports that hydroxyapatite prepared by microwave irradiation contains smaller particle size and closer size distribution [N3-F3]. In a study on ultralong hydroxyapatite, microwave hydrothermal synthesis at 140°C produces the crystalline phase of hydroxyapatite, but still retains an amorphous phase [N1-R2]. This suggests that microwave heating can promote crystallization but may still require careful optimization to fully convert the product into a crystalline phase. Across the evidence, the common theme is that microwave heating promotes faster and more uniform nucleation, reduces the time needed for crystal growth, and can produce more uniform particle size distributions than conventional hydrothermal synthesis [N1-F1][N3-F3].

The synthesis parameters that are optimized and why are centered around time, temperature, and sometimes pH. In the comparative hydrothermal and microwave irradiation study, pH and synthesis time were varied to determine optimal conditions [N3-R1]. In the same study, the hydrothermal method is associated with prolonged periods of time, while microwave irradiation can reach the required treatment temperature in fewer minutes [N3-F3]. In the vanadium neutralization slag study, the authors optimize microwave power, time, temperature, and raw material particle size to produce hydroxyapatite with desirable properties [N5-F4]. They also use response surface optimization to analyze and optimize various reaction parameters to promote an energy-efficient production process [N5-F4]. For conventional hydrothermal synthesis, the evidence emphasizes that reaction time, hydrothermal temperature, and pH are major factors determining the final product properties [N2-F2]. The reason these parameters are optimized is that they directly affect nucleation, crystal growth, crystallinity, morphology, and particle size [N2-F2]. In microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis, the same parameters are still relevant, but the heating mechanism changes the required optimization window: because heating is faster and more uniform, the reaction can be completed in shorter time at lower energy input [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-F4]. This makes microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis more attractive when the goal is rapid, energy-efficient production with controlled morphology and crystallinity.

Product quality and material properties differ between microwave-assisted hydrothermal and conventional hydrothermal synthesis in several ways, especially in crystallinity, morphology, particle size, purity, phase composition, and bioactivity or functional performance.

Crystallinity and morphology are the clearest differences. In the comparative hydrothermal and microwave irradiation study, the hydrothermal method was reported to produce hydroxyapatite nanoparticles that are relatively stoichiometric and present high crystallinity [N3-F3]. In contrast, the microwave irradiation method generally produces smaller particle size, good purity, and closer size distribution [N3-F3]. Another study on ultralong hydroxyapatite notes that microwave hydrothermal synthesis at 140°C produces the crystalline phase of hydroxyapatite, but there is still an amorphous phase [N1-R2]. This suggests that microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis can increase crystallinity relative to conventional hydrothermal methods, but the degree of crystallinity depends on the exact conditions. The same evidence also indicates that the hydrothermal method can produce hydroxyapatite with high crystallinity [N3-F3], so the difference is not that one method is inherently higher in crystallinity than the other, but that microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis can achieve comparable or even improved crystallinity under optimized conditions while producing smaller particles and more uniform morphology.

Particle size, purity, and phase composition are also affected. The comparative study reports that hydroxyapatite prepared by microwave irradiation generally contains smaller particle size and closer size distribution [N3-F3]. The same study also states that hydroxyapatite synthesized by hydrothermal methods can produce relatively stoichiometric and high-crystallinity nanoparticles [N3-F3]. The vanadium neutralization slag study further reports that microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis can produce high-purity hydroxyapatite with excellent adsorption properties, and that response surface optimization is used to tune synthesis conditions and improve product properties [N5-F4]. This implies that microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis can improve purity and phase composition by reducing unwanted side products and enhancing the desired hydroxyapatite phase. The evidence also suggests that the phase composition can be influenced by the feedstock and synthesis conditions, as the study notes that the hydrothermal method can produce homogeneous HAP from neutralization slag without the need for surfactants [N5-F4].

Bioactivity and functional performance are influenced by morphology and crystallinity. The hydrothermal synthesis study reports that the hydrothermal method presented more satisfactory morphological results according to TEM analysis and was considered more suitable as a route to obtain hydroxyapatite as a biomaterial [N3-F3]. The same study also notes that bioactivity evaluation showed high bioactivity due to the formation of apatite on the surface of the synthesized nanopowder [N2-F2]. The microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis in the fermented fish by-product study is described as a waste-to-resource route for producing hydroxyapatite with the potential to enhance adsorption kinetics, capacity, and reusability [N1-F1]. The vanadium neutralization slag study similarly emphasizes that the microwave-assisted process is proposed to produce high-purity hydroxyapatite with excellent adsorption properties and to optimize synthesis conditions for energy-efficient production [N5-F4]. Overall, microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis appears to favor smaller particle size, closer size distribution, and potentially higher bioactivity, while conventional hydrothermal synthesis may produce high-crystallinity materials but with different morphology and possibly larger particle size [N3-F3][N2-F2][N1-F1][N5-F4].

Practical advantages and limitations of microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis are clearest when comparing energy efficiency, time, scalability, cost, and equipment requirements.

Energy efficiency and time are among the strongest advantages. The evidence states that microwave-assisted hydrothermal processing delivers volumetric, homogeneous heating that accelerates nucleation and crystal growth, enabling shorter reaction times and lower energy input than conventional hydrothermal heating [N1-F1]. The comparative hydrothermal and microwave irradiation study similarly notes that microwave irradiation can reach the required treatment temperature in fewer minutes than the prolonged periods of time needed in the hydrothermal method [N3-F3]. The vanadium neutralization slag study explicitly frames the microwave-assisted process as a way to obtain high-purity hydroxyapatite with excellent adsorption properties and to optimize synthesis conditions for an energy-efficient production process [N5-F4]. This makes microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis particularly attractive for applications where rapid, energy-conscious synthesis is important.

Scalability is a key limitation. The evidence indicates that the hydrothermal method can have long reaction times and require elevated temperature and pressure, and that the reaction vessel has limited capacity per run, resulting in unsatisfactory saturation adsorption performance and increased synthesis cost [N5-F4]. In contrast, microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis is often described as more energy-efficient and rapid, but the same evidence also points to challenges in scaling up. The comparative study notes that microwave-assisted methods can provide a viable solution for reducing energy consumption and enhancing HAP [N5-R1], while the broader microwave-assisted synthesis literature indicates that scaling microwave-assisted reactions is difficult and requires approaches such as continuous-flow reactors, small-scale batch stop-flow protocols, or large-scale single-pulse reactors [N6-R2]. This suggests that while microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis is efficient at the lab scale, scaling to industrial production remains a challenge.

Cost and equipment requirements are mixed. The vanadium neutralization slag study emphasizes that the microwave method can use ordinary glass containers and reduce energy consumption compared to the hydrothermal method, but it also notes that the potential drawbacks include uneven temperature distribution, precise parameter control challenges, equipment damage risks, and elevated production costs [N5-F4]. The same study reports that the hydrothermal method can produce homogeneous HAP from neutralization slag without surfactants, but also has long reaction times and limited vessel capacity per run, increasing synthesis cost [N5-F4]. The microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis literature similarly suggests that microwave-assisted methods are powerful and versatile for nanomaterials, but scaling microwave-assisted reactions is difficult and requires specialized equipment and careful control [N6-R2][N6-R5]. So the practical trade-off is that microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis can lower energy and operating costs in some cases, but may require more expensive equipment and careful optimization to avoid uneven heating, precise parameter control issues, and equipment damage [N5-F4][N6-R2].

Remaining challenges and trade-offs include uneven temperature distribution, precise parameter control, equipment damage, and higher production costs for microwave-assisted methods [N5-F4][N6-R2]. At the same time, the hydrothermal method can produce high-crystallinity materials and is sometimes considered suitable for obtaining hydroxyapatite as a biomaterial [N3-F3], but it can be slow, energy-intensive, and limited by vessel capacity and reaction time [N5-F4]. Thus, the main trade-off is between speed and energy efficiency on one hand, and scalability, cost, and equipment requirements on the other [N5-F4][N6-R2].

The core difference is the heating mechanism: conventional hydrothermal synthesis relies on bulk heating through the vessel wall, while microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis delivers volumetric, homogeneous heating that accelerates nucleation and crystal growth [N1-F1][N3-F3]. This indicates that microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis is a variant of hydrothermal synthesis, but one that uses microwave energy transfer to change the reaction kinetics and optimize synthesis conditions differently.

Reproducibility and scale-up are addressed in the literature mainly through optimization and controlled synthesis design. The comparative hydrothermal and microwave irradiation study uses pH and synthesis time as variables to determine optimal conditions [N3-R1]. The vanadium neutralization slag study uses response surface optimization to analyze and optimize various reaction parameters, including microwave power, time, temperature, and raw material particle size, in order to promote an energy-efficient production process [N5-F4]. This means reproducibility is achievable with careful optimization, but scale-up is not trivial and depends on reactor design and process engineering.

The method is not route-specific in the sense that microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis can be applied to different feedstocks and reaction systems. The evidence includes examples from fermented fish by-product synthesis [N1-F1], eggshell-based synthesis [N3-F3], and vanadium neutralization slag [N5-F4], suggesting that the method can be adapted to different precursors and waste streams [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-F4]. At the same time, the method is broadly transferable only when the synthesis parameters and heating conditions are properly adjusted. The comparative study shows that pH and synthesis time are important variables that must be optimized for each system [N3-R1], and the vanadium neutralization slag study uses response surface optimization to tune conditions for a specific feedstock [N5-F4]. This indicates that the method is broadly applicable, but the exact route details depend on the feedstock, target morphology, and desired properties [N3-F3][N5-F4]. Overall, microwave-assisted hydrothermal synthesis is a route-specific variant of hydrothermal synthesis that is broadly transferable across feedstocks and applications, provided the synthesis parameters are optimized accordingly [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-F4][N6-R2].
